Rewire narrate, assemble and scan onto the typed loader
Three parsers become zero. All three now live inside `packages/openthrottle-showroom`, so this is intra-package rewiring rather than a cross-boundary import.

## Replace

- **`narrate/parse-script.ts`** — delete the file reading and front-matter regex; `parseScript(slug, variant?)` becomes a thin adapter over `getVariant` + the `sentences` helper, keeping the existing `ParsedScript` / `NarrationSentence` return shape so `narrate.ts`, the render cache and the timings writer need no changes beyond the variant plumbing.
- **`assemble/assemble.ts`** — drop the three regexes (`^title:`, `^titleCard:`, and the `/^ {2}- (.+)$/gm` tag scrape that matches any two-space bullet in the file). Read `episode.youtube.title`, `episode.production.titleCard` and `episode.youtube.tags` directly. The hardcoded description block moves out in favour of the composition helper.
- **`scan/leak-scan.ts`** — it reads `metadata.json` and the `.srt`; confirm it still resolves both once outputs are variant-namespaced, and update its path resolution if not.

## Narration matching becomes time-based — the substantial part

`assemble/timeline.ts` matches narration to flow beats **positionally**: nth narration sentence to nth flow beat. The 05 flow carries a comment warning that an extra flow beat "does not merely go unnarrated — it shifts every later beat's narration one beat early".

The typed format makes that untenable, and deliberately so. A variant owns its own timings — narration is a list of `['0:09', 'the words']` cues, independent of the episode's beats, because nothing says a slower payoff-first read speaks at a problem-first read's moments. There is no longer an nth-to-nth correspondence to rely on.

Replace it with a time-based reconciliation:

- The runner's `manifest.json` stays the authority on when a beat **actually** happened. Script and cue times are intent; captured spans are fact.
- Map each cue onto the beat span its `t` falls within, then keep the existing rule that governs the result: where a beat's narration runs longer than its on-screen action, **extend the dwell on the last frame** rather than speeding the picture up. Sped-up picture is the loudest "this was automated" tell there is.
- A cue whose time falls outside every captured span is an error worth naming, not a silently dropped line.

This removes the positional hazard rather than relocating it. Cover it with tests over a fixture manifest — this is the part of the rewiring most likely to be quietly wrong, and a wrong answer here means narration drifting against picture in a shipped video.

## Watch for

- `runner/format.ts` owns `repositoryRoot()` and `outputRoot()`. Do not grow a second copy of either alongside the episode helpers.
- `runner/run.ts` resolves flows by dynamic import template `../flows/${flowId}.flow.ts`. Co-located episodes make that `../episodes/${id}/flow.ts`.
- Anything still importing the old `tests/demo/**` paths.

## Done when

A narrate → assemble run for one migrated episode produces byte-identical narration text and an equivalent `metadata.json` to a pre-migration run, the three regexes are gone, and the timeline's cue-to-beat mapping is covered by tests.
DONE — three regex parsers gone, cues match beats by time in both timeline and captions, 10 new tests. Episode 05 narrates again and --variant works. Commit fbb6b508.

## The symptom

On all three legs of PR #402, the developer suite's Vitest summary is **missing**:

4. Update the PR checklist item if the shape of the evidence changes.

Plan-detail tabs: stop scroll position shifting on tab change
## Problem

On the plan detail route ([`applications/openthrottle-developer/app/routes/plans.$planId._index.tsx`](applications/openthrottle-developer/app/routes/plans.$planId._index.tsx)), clicking a tab (`overview` / `tasks` / `output` / `configuration`) shifts the page scroll position. The tabs are URL-linked, so navigation is expected to preserve scroll — it does not.

## Root cause is NOT the obvious one

These tabs are **not** React Router `<Link>`/`<NavLink>` elements — they are Radix/shadcn `TabsTrigger` buttons whose selection is synced to a search param. The `setSearchParams` call **already** passes `{ preventScrollReset: true }`, so the router-scroll-reset is already suppressed:

- Tabs component: [`PlanDetailRoute.tsx:113-158`](applications/openthrottle-developer/app/routing/plans/components/PlanDetailRoute.tsx) → `OpenThrottleTabs` (`packages/react-router-ui/src/components/OpenThrottleTabs.tsx`) → `OpenThrottleTabsWithUrlSync.tsx`.
- Navigation call: [`packages/react-router-ui/src/hooks/useUrlSyncedTabValue.ts:56`](packages/react-router-ui/src/hooks/useUrlSyncedTabValue.ts) — `setSearchParams(nextParams, { preventScrollReset: true })`.

So adding `preventScrollReset` is a no-op — it's there. The remaining scroll shift comes from something else. Likely candidates to verify:

1. **Radix focus-on-select**: when a tab is activated, Radix moves focus to the selected `TabsTrigger` (or the panel), and the browser scrolls that element into view. Check whether `focus({ preventScroll: true })` or `scroll-margin`/focus handling is needed.
2. **Layout/height change between panels**: the four panels have different heights; switching to a shorter panel can shrink the document and reflow scroll. Confirm by measuring `document.scrollingElement.scrollTop` before/after a tab click across panels of differing heights.

## Desired behavior

Clicking any plan-detail tab updates the active panel (and the URL param) **without** changing the window scroll position — the toolbar/tab strip stays exactly where it was.

## Scope note

The tab wiring is shared (`OpenThrottleTabsWithUrlSync` / `useUrlSyncedTabValue` in `@openthrottle/react-router-ui`), so a fix here benefits every URL-synced tab surface. Prefer a fix in the shared hook/component over a route-local patch, and keep the existing `preventScrollReset: true`.

## Verification

- Reproduce on `plans.$planId._index.tsx` with the window scrolled partway down, then click across all four tabs; scroll offset must not change.
- Diagnose which of the two causes applies (add a temporary `scrollTop` log or inspect focus target) before committing a fix, so the change targets the actual mechanism.
- Update/extend the `useUrlSyncedTabValue` / `OpenThrottleTabs` tests if the fix changes their behavior.
On applications/openthrottle-developer/app/routes/plans.$planId._index.tsx the URL-synced tabs jump the scroll position when a tab is clicked. Note: the setSearchParams call already passes { preventScrollReset: true } (useUrlSyncedTabValue.ts:56), so the router is NOT the cause — investigate the real culprit (Radix focus-scroll on the newly-shown TabsTrigger/panel, or layout/height change between panels) and stop the jump.

Map word timings to sentence boundaries and slice the take
The bridge between a single take and everything downstream. Consume the word stream in order against the per-sentence SPOKEN text (lexicon-substituted; normalise case and punctuation for matching only) to find each sentence's first and last word.

Cut placement matters: cutting at a word's exact end clips breath and consonant tails. Cut at the midpoint of the gap between the last word of sentence N and the first word of N+1 (falling back to the next word's start when there is no measurable gap), so nothing audible is lost and the sentences still sum to the take.

Slice with ffmpeg into the SAME `NNN-<beat>.wav` names the per-sentence path produces, and write the same `timings.json`. `assemble/timeline.ts` and `assemble/captions.ts` must not need edits — that is the acceptance test.

Desync is the real risk: lexicon substitution turns 'MCP' into 'M C P', which the service may return as one word or three. When the word stream cannot be reconciled with the sentence text, FAIL with the sentence index and the words it could not match — do not fall back to proportional splitting, which drifts silently and shows up later as captions landing on the wrong line.

Merge-driven reconciliation: PR merge → work-ledger artifact → plan/task status settle
## The problem
Every plan run ends with the same manual ritual: after the PR merges, someone must attach_session_subject + record_artifact the squash commit, and flip the plan to COMPLETED — and it routinely doesn't happen. Evidence: a long trail of plans annotated "DONE PR #NNN (unmerged, ledger owed)" in the planning record (e.g. 677dcaab global help modal, 082bf81f scheduled-job run detail, 0cbfffd3 onboarding-in-a-modal, de854c29 appearance regroup); a one-time 506-row commit_links backfill was already needed to reconcile main; and there is a known gap that nothing server-side downward-reconciles a plan whose tasks are all COMPLETED — plans strand. Meanwhile 97 of the last 100 PRs are merged, so the debt is pure bookkeeping, not blocked work. The ingredients now exist: the work ledger shipped (#195/#198/#199/#200) and run provenance shipped on plan_runs — branch, worktree, model, PR linkage (#280) — but nothing consumes that provenance.

## The proposed change
A reconciliation service in openthrottle-server (BullMQ repeatable job first; GitHub webhook later if wanted) that: (1) polls the canonical repo (gh/GitHub API) for merged PRs matching plan_runs' recorded branch/PR provenance from #280; (2) on merge, opens a system work-ledger session and records the squash commit as a git_commit artifact against the plan (and task where resolvable via Plan-Id:/Task-Id: footers); (3) settles status: a plan with all tasks COMPLETED plus a merged PR flips to COMPLETED, stamped with a system actor and an audit note. Surface reconciliation results in the developer app plan detail ("merged via #NNN on <date>"). Mirrors the already-accepted heartbeat/staleness pattern for stranded runs (#226) — this is the same idea applied to the ledger and terminal statuses.

## What it unlocks
Removes the per-plan manual ledger/status step entirely (the single most repeated piece of process debt on record); makes the work ledger trustworthy enough to build on (activity timeline, Institutional Memory theme on roadmap ce7e2773); eliminates future backfills; gives the ten recurring Job_* audit jobs accurate plan-state input.

## Rough size
3–5 days. Touches openthrottle-server (new module + repeatable job), databases (possibly a reconciliation audit column/table), openthrottle-mcp (optional read surface), openthrottle-developer (plan-detail provenance display).

## Migration risk
Low — additive service over existing tables. Risks: mis-attribution when one PR covers several plans or a plan spans several PRs (mitigate: only auto-settle on unambiguous provenance, otherwise flag for review); GitHub API rate limits (poll interval + etag caching). Rollback: disable the repeatable job; no schema unwinding required if audit data is additive.

## The strongest argument against
A merged PR does not always mean the plan's intent shipped — partial implementations, reverted merges, and follow-up PRs are real, and an automated COMPLETED flip can quietly mislabel work, which is worse than a stranded IN_PROGRESS because nobody re-checks a completed plan. For a single-operator system the manual step costs a minute, and the honest fix might be discipline (or the existing skills prompting for it) rather than new always-on infrastructure that itself must be monitored.

Add a package-entrypoint consistency guard to CI

Design the typed episode shape
Design task — output is a short design note plus the type file skeleton, not a migration.

## Decide the type shape

Start from every field the three current parsers read, plus the fields `docs/marketing/publishing.md` and `docs/marketing/youtube-format.md` describe but nobody stores. Group them:

- **identity** — `id` (slug, matches the flow id), `format: 'short' | 'longform'`.
- **production** — `recording: 'live' | 'replay'`, `flow` (demo flow id), `titleCard: readonly [string, string]`, `blockedOn: readonly string[]`, optional `portraitStrategy` if it belongs here rather than on the flow.
- **release** — `order: number` (today's `release`), `status: 'draft' | 'ready' | 'recorded' | 'published'`, `playlist` (one of the four in `publishing.md`), optional `publishedUrl` / `publishedAt`.
- **youtube** — `title`, `summary` (the per-video paragraph that opens the description), `tags`, `chapters` (long-form only), optional `thumbnail: { words: readonly string[] }`.
- **variants** — `readonly Variant[]` plus `selectedVariant: string`.

Build the @openthrottle/nodejs-parts-department package
Scaffold with the `package` generator (`--type=node`), never by hand:

```bash
NX_ISOLATE_PLUGINS=false pnpm nx g @tools/generators:package --organization=@openthrottle --type=node --name=nodejs-parts-department
```

`--type=node` selects the plain-Node package template (`tools/generators/src/generators/package/files/node`) — not `nestjs`, `react`, or `tools`. `--organization=@openthrottle` puts it at `packages/nodejs-parts-department` as `@openthrottle/nodejs-parts-department`; the generator derives the destination from the name verbatim, so the slug must be the full `nodejs-parts-department`. Run `--describe` first if the option set has moved.

Implement exactly the API settled in task 1. Non-negotiables:

- **Zero runtime dependencies.** If it needs an import, the design is wrong.
- **`.subsetOf()` is the load-bearing piece.** Its parameter must be an exhaustive `Record<Member, boolean>` so omitting a member is a compile error. This is what converts today's silently-excluding arrays into a forced decision.
- **`.labelled()`** takes an exhaustive `Record<Member, string>`.
- Explicit return types; no `as` casts; no `any`; `as const` objects rather than TS enums (repo style — note the generated GraphQL enums are the pre-existing exception, not a licence for new ones).
- Public API needs JSDoc `@public` or Knip strips it.
- Keep whatever the `node` template emits for source-first packaging (`main`/`types` → `./src/index.ts`, `__build` placeholder, no real `build` target) rather than hand-adjusting it; if the template disagrees with task 1's decision, reconcile in the plan output before editing.

**Type-level tests matter more than runtime tests here.** The whole value is the compile error. Assert the negative cases — an incomplete `labelled()` map and an incomplete `subsetOf()` map must both fail to typecheck. Runtime assertions alone would pass even if the types silently widened to `string`, which is precisely the bug this package exists to prevent. Use `@ts-expect-error` (it fails the build when the error does NOT occur, making it a real assertion) or a `tsd`-style approach if one is already in the repo — check before adding a dependency.

4. Developer SSR: shrink ide-engine.server chunk (11.95 MB)
## Finding
The SSR server build ships an **11.95 MB** `ide-engine.server` chunk (gzip **2042.7 KB**). First IDE request pays a multi-megabyte module load even though routes dynamic-import it.

## Paths
- `applications/openthrottle-developer/app/routing/ide/data/ide-engine.server.ts`
- Routes: `ide._index.tsx`, `ide.files.tsx`, `ide.symbol.tsx`, `ide.symbols.tsx` (dynamic `import('~/routing/ide/data/ide-engine.server')`)
- Built: `applications/openthrottle-developer/build/server/assets/ide-engine.server-*.js`
- Likely weight from `packages/openthrottle-ide` / TypeScript language services

## Measured before
```bash
pnpm nx run openthrottle-developer:build
# ide-engine.server-*.js = 11674.2 KB raw / 2042.7 KB gzip-9
# build/server total ≈ 25 MB; index.js 4653 KB
```

## Suspected cause
Bundling a full IDE/analysis engine into the React Router SSR server output instead of keeping it external or in a separate Node worker process.

## Proposed fix
Mark heavy IDE deps `ssr.external` / load via Node `createRequire` outside the Vite SSR bundle; or move analysis to a dedicated service. Keep the route-level dynamic import.

## Expected after
`ide-engine.server-*.js` **≤ 2 MB raw** (or absent from SSR assets with equivalent functionality via external require). Server build dir **≤ 15 MB**.

## Acceptance
Re-measure after production build: `ide-engine.server-*.js` raw size ≤ 2048 KB, or documented external load with SSR asset gone.

Decide the queue's config surface, merge method, and tuning knobs (human gate)

Which surface owns the queue.** `main` is protected TWICE today: classic branch protection (holds the only required check, `ci-success`) and ruleset id 14604876 (holds `required_linear_history`, `non_fast_forward`, `deletion`, and `pull_request` with `allowed_merge_methods: ["rebase"]`). Rulesets support a `merge_queue` rule; classic protection has its own "Require merge queue" toggle. Pick ONE and say why. Recommendation: put the `merge_queue` rule in the ruleset (it is already the richer, API-manageable surface) and, in a follow-up, move `required_status_checks: [ci-success]` there too so there is a single place to read — but do NOT move the required check in the same change as enabling the queue, so a stall has one candidate cause, not two.

**2. Queue merge method.** `MERGE` is ruled out by `required_linear_history`. Choose `SQUASH` or `REBASE` and state the consequence for commit shape. The repo's conventional-commit + `Plan-Id:`/`Task-Id:` footer convention (CLAUDE.md § Git and agent behavior) is the constraint: with `SQUASH`, repo settings `squash_merge_commit_title: PR_TITLE` + `squash_merge_commit_message: COMMIT_MESSAGES` decide what survives; with `REBASE`, every individual commit lands and each must already be conventional. - `merge_method`
- `max_entries_to_build` (how many entries build speculatively in parallel)
- `min_entries_to_merge` / `max_entries_to_merge` (batch size)
- `min_entries_to_merge_wait_minutes`
- `check_response_timeout_minutes` — must exceed the CI worst case. 3. Developer client: remove 8.66 MB orphan Monaco workers
## Finding
Monaco language workers are emitted into the **client** build but are referenced by **zero** client JS modules — 70% of client JS is dead deploy weight.

## Paths
- Built orphans: `applications/openthrottle-developer/build/client/assets/{ts,css,html,json}.worker-*.js`
- Related: `packages/react-router-editor` (Monaco); `packages/react-router-editor/AGENTS.md` notes apps do not configure `MonacoEnvironment` / `?worker` imports
- Server copies the same workers under `build/server/assets/`

## Measured before
After `pnpm nx run openthrottle-developer:build`:
- Workers total **8.66 MB** of **12.31 MB** client JS (70.3%)
- Per file: ts 6731.7 / css 1029.7 / html 702.6 / json 399.5 KB
- Grep of all non-worker client JS for worker hashes / `ts.worker` / `MonacoEnvironment`: **NONE**

```bash
pnpm nx run openthrottle-developer:build
python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
a=Path('applications/openthrottle-developer/build/client/assets')
ws=list(a.glob('*worker*.js'))
print(sum(p.stat().st_size for p in ws)/1024/1024, 'MB', len(ws), 'files')
PY
```

## Suspected cause
SSR/client asset emission of Monaco worker files without a client `MonacoEnvironment` wiring them; RR may be copying server assets into `build/client`.

## Proposed fix
Stop emitting unreferenced workers into `build/client`. If self-hosted Monaco is desired, wire `MonacoEnvironment` + `?worker` only on editor routes (prompts/plans/skills) and keep workers out of the default client graph; otherwise leave CDN path explicit and delete the orphans.

## Expected after
Client `*worker*.js` count **0**, or workers only appear as dependencies of an editor route chunk that actually imports them. Client JS total **≤ ~4 MB** (≈ current excl-workers 3.65 MB).

## Acceptance
Re-run measure: orphan worker bytes in `build/client/assets` = **0**, or every worker file is referenced by ≥1 non-worker client module.

11. Developer shell: keep react-markdown/acorn (505.6 KB) off every route
## Finding
Discovered while doing task 2. The developer app's root shell statically pulls a **505.6 KB** chunk that Rolldown names `MarkdownRenderer-*.js`. Fingerprinting it found **two copies of acorn** (`tryReadTemplateToken`, `` `Using declaration is not allowed in single-statement positions` ``), an astring-style code generator, and micromark character tables — i.e. a complete JavaScript parser plus the react-markdown/MDX pipeline, downloaded on every navigation.

This is now the single largest item in the developer base shell.

## Paths
- Static importer inside root's graph: `chat-toolbar-reconcile-*.js` (75.3 KB) -> `MarkdownRenderer-*.js`
- `packages/react-router-markdown/src/**` (`MarkdownRenderer`)
- `packages/react-router-chat/src/**` (chat toolbar / message rendering reached from `GlobalLayoutHeader`'s ChatDialog)
- `applications/openthrottle-developer/app/root.tsx`

Other static importers (legitimately markdown-rendering routes, fine to keep): `plans.$planId._index`, `plans.$planId.tasks.$taskId._index`, `notes.$noteId`, `docs._index`, `skills.$slug`, `faq._index`, `schedule.$jobId._index`, `OutputStream`, `DocPageView`.

## Measured before
```bash
pnpm nx run openthrottle-developer:build --skip-nx-cache
```
Root transitive **static** graph = **1207.6 KB raw / 381.4 KB gzip** (114 chunks), of which `MarkdownRenderer-*.js` is **505.6 KB** — 42%.

Confirm the edge with:
```bash
# list chunks that STATICALLY (not dynamically) import the markdown chunk
# see the graph walker used in this plan's task-2 notes
```

## Suspected cause
The global header mounts the chat surface eagerly; chat message rendering statically imports `MarkdownRenderer`, so the markdown/MDX stack is hoisted into the shared shell chunk rather than staying on the routes that actually render prose.

## Proposed fix
`React.lazy` the markdown renderer at the chat-message boundary (same pattern as `GlobalMetricsChart` in task 2), so the shell keeps only the chat chrome. Verify whether the MDX/acorn path is needed at all — if the renderer only handles CommonMark, dropping the MDX plugin removes both acorn copies outright.

## Expected after
- `MarkdownRenderer-*.js` **not** in the static import graph of `root-*.js`
- Root transitive static graph **≤ 750 KB raw**
- Markdown-rendering routes (`plans.*`, `docs.*`, `notes.*`, `skills.*`) still render prose correctly

## Acceptance
Production build: `root-*.js` has no static path to the markdown chunk, root static graph ≤ 750 KB raw, and `openthrottle-developer:test` stays green.

Decide how a terminal-and-editor short is captured
## Decision: option A — typeset the shell in the recording browser

Rejected B (reshoot around `/settings/mcp`): the short's subject is wiring an agent CLI so it can write plans. `/settings/mcp` is the dashboard's connector catalogue — a different feature. Reshooting there does not make the short cheaper, it makes it a different short, and 06/07 already need the dashboard.

Rejected C (real terminal capture): `spike/README.md` settled Playwright over screen capture, and nothing in this script is evidence against that decision. It would also put the operator's real shell — scrollback included — in frame, which is the exact failure the fixture-only database exists to prevent.

## How option A is built

Two new verbs in `runner/types.ts` + `runner/actions.ts`, both of which read as on-screen actions in a script's action column:

- `stage(name)` — put a typeset surface on camera via `page.setContent`. Surfaces are declared on the flow (`DemoFlow.surfaces`, name → HTML) and reach `runStep` through `ActionContext.surfaces`. NOT a `navigate`: `navigate` waits on `#ot-env` for app hydration, which a static surface does not have and should not fake.
- `reveal(selector)` — un-hide an element staged with `data-demo-hidden`. This is what makes "the printed block appears", "the paste lands" and "the agent replies" single steps instead of four near-duplicate surface variants. Hidden elements are `display:none`, so they are absent from `innerText` and therefore absent from the beat's leak-scan dump until the beat that actually puts them on screen — which is the correct semantics, not a workaround.

`installCursor` is self-contained (it injects its own stylesheet and SVG), so the synthetic cursor, the click ring and `__demo_highlight` all work on a staged surface with no change.

## The output on camera is the real command's real output

`scripts/setup_mcp-instructions.ts` already exports `renderInstructions(root, status)` as a pure function, precisely so it can be asserted without parsing colorised stdout. The terminal surface calls it. So the block the viewer is told to copy is generated by the same code path `pnpm run setup:mcp-instructions` runs — it cannot drift from the product the way a hand-pasted mock would — while `root` and `status` stay under the recording's control. chalk emits no ANSI when stdout is not a TTY, so the string arrives as plain text.

This is what makes A strictly better than a mock, and it is what resolves tasks 2 and 3 without touching the script's behaviour.

## Script correction the decision forces

Beat 0:15 as written ("Editor opens `.mcp.json`; paste the block; save") describes a surface the command does not produce. `setup_mcp-instructions.ts` prints, for Claude Code, a single `claude mcp add-json … --scope user` command line; the paste-into-a-file branch is Cursor's `~/.cursor/mcp.json`. The short's title, title card and narration are all Claude Code, so the beat follows the Claude Code branch: copy the printed command, run it in the same terminal. The editor leaves the short entirely.

That also removes an editor pane from the frame, which is the surface most likely to carry a path — a welcome side effect given task 2.
DECIDED: option A. Typeset surfaces via page.setContent + two new verbs (stage, reveal); terminal output comes from the real renderInstructions() export, not a mock.

Deliverable: a short decision record captured on this task so the downstream tasks have unambiguous inputs.
DECISION RECORD (task-1 gate).

1) Install descriptor shape on AgentDriver (packages/openthrottle-drivers/src/types/index.ts, keep leaf dep-free):
   install?: { method: 'curl-shell'; url: string; installerShell: 'bash' | 'sh' }
   update?:  { method: 'curl-shell' } | { method: 'command'; argv: readonly string[] }   // argv = args AFTER the binary; command runs `<binary> <argv...>`

2) Per-CLI install URL/shell (from setup_software.sh) + researched update:
   claude   install https://claude.ai/install.sh (bash)      update: command ['update']   (`claude update`, native updater)
   cursor   install https://cursor.com/install (bash)         update: curl-shell (re-run installer; auto-updates by default, `cursor-agent update` ambiguous — re-run is robust & idempotent)
   codex    install https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh (sh) update: command ['update']   (`codex update`, confirmed 2026)
   grok     install https://x.ai/cli/install.sh (bash)        update: command ['update']   (`grok update`)
   opencode install https://opencode.ai/install (bash)        update: command ['upgrade']  (`opencode upgrade`)

3) Permission: REUSE existing SETTINGS_WRITE ('settings:write') from @openthrottle/nestjs-rbac — it already exists and is DB-seeded (migration 034); ADMIN has it. No new permission / no new seed migration. (Read-only status view keeps SETTINGS_READ.) Note drift: migration 034 grants settings:write only to admin, not the `user` role — acceptable, install is admin+env-gated.

4) Env flag: OT_AGENT_CLI_INSTALL_ENABLED, DEFAULT-OFF. Read via ConfigService.get<string>()?.trim().toLowerCase(), enabled only for 'true'|'1'|'yes' (mirror readAgentsChatMutationsEnabledFromConfig). When disabled the mutation resolves a typed { ok:false, disabled:true } result and NEVER spawns. UI shows controls disabled + reason. Read-only view ignores the flag.

5) Execution/streaming: sync mutation returns a runId, live stdout/stderr via graphql-ws @Subscription mirroring conversation-stream (pubSub topic agent-setup:<runId>:stream, chunk @ObjectType, buffered replay). NOT BullMQ. Bounded timeout (~10min) + AbortSignal; v1 may skip a cancel mutation. PATH gotcha: executor must augment child env PATH with common install target dirs (~/.local/bin, ~/.bun/bin, ~/.opencode/bin, ~/.cursor/bin, etc.) so post-install discovery sees the new binary. On success call AgentDiscoveryService cache.invalidate() so next discoverAgentClis re-scans.

Placement: descriptors in openthrottle-drivers (task 2, pure data); executor as new file in agentic-utils conversation-backend with an injectable spawn seam (task 3); server mutations+subscription in a NEW sibling `agent-setup` GraphQL module, leaving agent-discovery read-only (task 4).

Server: resolve an absolute path to one of the caller's registered checkouts
Add a small, user-scoped service that answers "which of this user's registered checkouts contains this path?" — the primitive everything else in this plan builds on.

## Shape

`resolveCheckoutForPath({ path, userId })` → `{ checkoutId, repositoryId } | null`.

- Reject anything that is not an absolute path up front (return `null`, do not throw).
- Realpath-normalize both the input path and each checkout's `filesystemPath` before comparing, so a symlinked workspace cannot make a registered checkout look unregistered. `worktree-discovery.service.ts` already does exactly this (`indexCheckouts` keys on `realPath(checkout.filesystemPath)`) — reuse the same helper rather than writing a second normalizer.
- Match on path containment, **deepest match wins**. A registered worktree nested under a registered primary checkout must resolve to the worktree, not the primary. Compare on path segment boundaries so `/repo-two` never matches under `/repo`.
- List checkouts with the existing user-scoped `checkoutsService.listByUserId`.
- Total function: unknown path, no checkouts, or a filesystem error all return `null`.

## Definition of done

- Unit tests cover: exact checkout path; a nested subdirectory of a checkout; a symlinked path; a registered worktree nested inside a registered primary (deepest wins); a sibling path sharing a prefix (`/repo-two` vs `/repo`) not matching; a relative path; a path under no checkout; a user with zero checkouts; and a checkout belonging to a *different* user never matching.
- `pnpm nx run openthrottle-server:test` and `:typecheck` pass.

Make usePlanOutputStream tolerate a late snapshot
`app/routing/plans/hooks/usePlanOutputStream.tsx` takes `(planId, loaderSnapshot)` and merges `planOutputChunkAdded` deltas onto the snapshot. Today the snapshot is present on first render. With `outputChunks` deferred, the subscription can (and on an actively-running plan, will) deliver chunks before the snapshot lands.

Change the merge so it is order-independent:
- Keep live deltas in state from mount, regardless of snapshot availability — the subscription must NOT wait for the snapshot, or output written during the load window is lost until the next revalidation.
- When the snapshot resolves, union it with the already-received deltas, **deduped by chunk `id`**, sorted by `iteration` then `createdAt` (the resolver returns `createdAt: 'ASC'`).
- Re-resolution on revalidation must not resurrect chunks or reorder the stream.

Decide and document where the hook is called: keeping it inside the Output tab's `Await` boundary is simplest but tears down the subscription when the tab is unmounted; calling it above the boundary keeps the stream alive across tab switches. Given the Output tab is the point of the subscription, pick one, write the reason in the hook's JSDoc, and make the choice consistent with the bounded `limit: 200` tail from the query split.

Capability matrix: hook and plugin surfaces across all five agent CLIs
Direction-independent research. For each of claude, codex, cursor, opencode, grok — the five in `packages/openthrottle-drivers/src/drivers/` — establish:

1. Does it support hooks at all, and at which lifecycle points?
2. Where is hook config read from (in-repo file, home dir, both)?
3. Is there any **out-of-repo** override — a settings flag, a plugin dir, an env var — or must config live inside the working tree?
4. Is there a plugin/extension mechanism that bundles hooks?

Known starting points: claude has `--settings`, `--plugin-dir`, `--plugin-url`, and a plugin marketplace (verified via `claude --help`). Cursor reads `.cursor/hooks.json` in-repo (`version: 1`, `afterFileEdit` / `beforeSubmitPrompt`) — we already ship one adapter there. The other three are unknown.

Deliverable: a table in `docs/monorepo/`, mirroring the CLI table in §2 of `foreign-workspace-skill-injection.md`. This directly answers whether the overlay is one mechanism or a per-CLI fan-out, and it is the only thing that could rescue option C.
Matrix at `docs/monorepo/agent-cli-hook-capability-matrix.md`. All five CLIs were installed on this machine, so every row was established by RUNNING the binary (claude 2.1.232, codex-cli 0.147.0, cursor-agent 2026.08.11, opencode 1.18.16, grok 1.0.0), not read off a docs site. HEADLINE, AND IT INVERTS THE SKILLS PRECEDENT: every one of the five has an out-of-repo hook config path — three via a home-directory config layer, two via a per-invocation directory flag. §2 of the skill-injection record found that NO CLI exposes an out-of-repo skills directory, which is what forced materialization into the target tree; hooks are the opposite. This permanently closes option C, which was only rescuable if some CLI had no out-of-repo hook config AND parity became a v1 requirement — neither half holds. TWO FINDINGS CONTRADICT THE PLAN'S ASSUMPTIONS. (1) cursor-agent ALSO accepts `--plugin-dir`, repeatable, exactly like Claude; the plan had it as in-repo-only. Leg B generalizes to cursor with no new mechanism, since `capabilities.pluginDir` and `appendPluginDirShellFlags` are already per-driver — it is a payload plus flipping one boolean. (2) grok LOADS Claude plugins (`grok inspect` listed ours as "openthrottle (user, enabled) hooks" the moment it was installed) but does NOT fire them — verified on a headless run that provably used the skill and produced no event. Two structural reasons: hook execution requires per-project trust whose only lever is the interactive `/hooks-trust` slash command with no CLI flag, which blocks unattended foreign-repo runs by design; and grok has no `Skill` tool at all (`inspect` reports "unknown tool prefix: Skill") plus no `UserPromptExpansion`, so BOTH of our capture paths have nothing to match. Recorded loudly because "grok reads Claude plugins" is exactly the half-truth that would be mistaken for coverage. ALSO: codex needs no injection mechanism whatsoever — hooks live in `~/.codex/config.toml`, never in the repo (with `-c hooks.…`, `--profile`, `CODEX_HOME` for per-invocation control, and `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust` for automation). opencode is the only awkward one: its plugins are npm modules, not directories, so covering it is a publishing decision rather than a technical obstacle. Recommended order: claude (shipped) → cursor → codex → grok/opencode stay on option D. Machine state left clean — the test plugin and marketplace were uninstalled/removed.

Sanitize pass: deny list, secret detector, identity scrub, timestamp rebase
The export pipes every row through a sanitize stage before it reaches disk:

- **Deny-listed tables** never export regardless of FK closure: `mcp_connector_connections` and anything credential-adjacent (audit the schema for token/secret/credential columns and write the list down with reasons). A denied table that other exported rows FK into gets its FK column nulled or the dependent row dropped — decided per case in the manifest.
- **Secret detector, fail-closed**: known key shapes (AWS, GitHub, Anthropic/OpenAI, JWTs, private key blocks, connection strings with passwords) plus a high-entropy-string heuristic over all kept free text. A hit STOPS the export naming table, column and row id — no silent redaction. Accepted residual risk is explicit: this is best-effort; recordings are human-reviewed before publishing.
- **Identity scrub inside free text**: emails, `/Users/*` and `/home/*` paths, machine hostnames. Word-boundary replacement from a small committed mapping (e.g. real email → demo user email). GitHub usernames and repo names are KEPT deliberately — the repo is public and the workspace is expected to become public.
- **Timestamp rebase**: all timestamps rewritten to the existing minute-offset-from-seed-time convention (offset from the newest timestamp in the window), so a frozen snapshot renders as a fresh, recently-active workspace on camera. Preserve relative ordering exactly; keep plan_output_stream offsets strictly increasing and unique per plan.

Give the region-of-interest sample an explicit timeout and warn loudly when a region never resolves
`sampleRegion` in `runner/run.ts` calls `page.locator(selector).first().boundingBox().catch(() => null)`. A selector that never matches burns Playwright's 30s default timeout, the error is swallowed, and because nothing is added to `sampledBeats` it retries on EVERY subsequent step of that beat. One wrong selector turned a 54s recording into 264s with no error and no warning — the run reported success.

Fix:

- Pass a short explicit timeout to `boundingBox({ timeout })` — a region either exists at this moment or it does not. Add a named constant with a comment explaining the 30s-default trap.
- Track which declared `regionOfInterest` beats never resolved, and after the loop log a loud `run: WARNING` naming each unresolved beat and its selector, so a silent 5x inflation surfaces at the end of the run.
- Do not retry the same beat indefinitely: cap the attempts per beat so a bad selector costs bounded time rather than one timeout per step.

Acceptance: a flow with a deliberately bogus `regionOfInterest` selector finishes in roughly the same wall time as one with none, and prints a warning naming the beat and selector.

Seed a rule that can actually fire on camera
Nothing in this short works unless a seeded rule matches a seeded plan. Three preconditions, all currently unmet or unverified:

**The tag must be in the vocabulary.** `PlanTagChips.tsx` offers a `<select>` populated from `skillTagVocabulary` with an "Add tag…" placeholder and an Add button - it is not a free-text field. If `needs-review` is not in the vocabulary it cannot be picked on camera, and the 0:00 beat has no action.

**The plan owner must resolve to a users row.** The processor resolves the owner from `plan.author` (GitHub username) to a users row, and its own doc comment says "a plan whose author has no user row has no rules and is skipped". The demo records as `GITHUB_USER=atlas-ada`, so that user must exist and must own the seeded rules.

**The rule must be unqualified.** The v1 worker evaluates with `environment=null`, so an environment-qualified rule only matches on qualified read paths, not here. A seeded rule with an environment set will silently never fire.

Use `inject-task` as the action: it is one of only two action types (`summarizeRuleAction` in `app/routing/rules/utils/formatters.ts` handles `inject-task` and `availability-exception`) and the only one with a visible effect on a plan.

Extend `tests/demo/fixtures/demo-content.ts` and `scripts/seed-demo.ts` to write the rule, and confirm end to end that adding the tag by hand produces a ledger row and an injected task before any recording is attempted.

Set a real Vitest timeout budget across the workspace
**Root cause A.** `grep -rn testTimeout` across the repo (excluding node_modules) returns zero hits — no `vitest.config.ts`, no shared setup, no Nx targetDefault sets one. Every suite in the monorepo therefore runs on Vitest's 5000ms default with zero headroom, and the failures are all narrow overruns (the `Editor.ssr` case measured 6318ms against 5000ms), not hangs.

### Approach

Establish a shared base rather than sprinkling per-file `{ timeout: N }` arguments, which drift and hide the policy:

- Export a shared Vitest base (`testTimeout` and `hookTimeout`) that every project config merges in. `packages/react-router-testing` already serves this role for the four React Router apps via `setupReactRouterTest`, but node-side packages and `tools/generators` do not use it — so the base needs to be config-level, not setup-level, to cover both.
- Pick the budget from measurement, not taste: the observed overruns are 5–7s against 5000ms, and CI boxes now run 3 shards with higher per-box contention. **15000ms** for `testTimeout` gives ~2× headroom over the worst observed case without letting a genuine hang sit for a minute. Set `hookTimeout` to match, since `beforeAll` in the generator suites does the expensive tree setup.
- Raising the ceiling must not become cover for unbounded suites: keep the per-shard `timeout-minutes: 30` job ceiling as-is so a real hang still fails the box.

Explicitly rejected: blanket `retry: 1`. It converts a real timing regression into a silent 2× cost and a green check — the opposite of what this plan is for.

### Verify

Run the three offending projects with the new budget and confirm green, then confirm a deliberately-hung test still fails (temporarily add one, observe the 15s failure, remove it).

Related context: `docs/monorepo/ci-cost.md` records the measured shard economics; note the timeout choice there if that doc tracks CI tuning decisions.
No project sets testTimeout, so every suite runs on Vitest's 5000ms default; three I/O-heavy suites exceed it under CI load.

Retire the paid GCS Nx remote cache in favour of the free GitHub Actions cache
We pay GCS egress on every cache read while `.github/actions/node-setup` **already** caches `.nx/cache` through `actions/cache` — a free layer duplicating a paid one. On a public repo, GitHub Actions cache is free (10 GB/repo, LRU eviction).

**The security model survives for free.** GitHub Actions cache scoping already enforces exactly what the current setup achieves with `NX_POWERPACK_CACHE_MODE`: a PR branch can *read* caches from its base branch but cannot *write* into them, and branch caches are isolated from each other. That is the CREEP-safe (CVE-2025-36852) trusted-`main`-writes / PRs-read-only model, by construction, with no env override to maintain.

Work:
1. Strengthen the existing `actions/cache` step — the key is `hashFiles('nx.json','pnpm-lock.yaml')` with a loose `restore-keys` prefix, which is right for an Nx local cache. Verify `main` populates it and PRs restore from it.
2. Remove from `continuous-integration.yml`: the `🪣 NX Setup Cache` sed step, the `🌥️ Google Cloud Provider (GCP)` step, `NX_POWERPACK_CACHE_MODE`, `NX_GCS_BUCKET`, `GOOGLE_CREDENTIALS`, `GOOGLE_PROJECT_ID`. Same in `vercel-deploy.yml`.
3. Remove the `gcs` block from `nx.json` and drop `@nx/gcs-cache`. Confirm whether `NX_KEY` is still needed for anything else before removing it.
4. Keep the bucket for a couple of weeks, then delete it (90-day lifecycle otherwise pays storage for dead entries).

**Watch out:** `poisoned-gcs-nx-remote-cache` documents that gitignored `__generated__` output is invisible to Nx hashing. That hazard follows the cache, not the backend — it applies to the GitHub cache too, so keep the runbook and keep the codegen-before-affected ordering intact.

**Trade-off to state plainly:** 10 GB with LRU eviction is smaller than the 2.19 GB currently used but shared across all branches and workflows, so eviction pressure is higher; cross-branch hit rate may drop slightly. Measure hit rate before and after.

One bootstrap engine behind all four setup paths (setup.sh, Docker, worktree:new, CI) + doctor mode
## The problem
Setup/bootstrap was the single most-patched subsystem of the month: #290 (leak audit), #292 (dual-volume Postgres reset), #296 (one-command Docker bootstrap), #297 (MCP auth self-load), #298 (MCP config SSOT), #299 (env prep), #306 (MCP install script), #321 (bootstrap-secrets file + MCP setup skip + RBAC superset), #324 (ensure-migrations gate), #342 (admin permission backfill), #344 (guarantee all six .demo-workstation.local fields), #345/#346 (setup trim/polish) — roughly a dozen PRs in 30 days, each fixing drift between the four parallel install paths: ./scripts/setup.sh (local), the Dockerized bootstrap, pnpm run worktree:new provisioning (#271), and CI. Each path hand-maintains its own env, secrets, DB, migration, MCP-registration, and seed-user handling, so every fix lands in one path and the others drift until they break — the recorded gotchas (stale .env password symptom, MCP config shadowing, pinned-port fallbacks) are all instances of this. The repeated patching says the design, not the scripts, is what is wrong.

## The proposed change
A single bootstrap engine — a small typed CLI package (e.g. packages/openthrottle-bootstrap or under tools/) — that models setup as declarative, idempotent, individually-verifiable steps: env file materialization, secrets (the six bootstrap-secrets fields as a schema, not a convention), Docker services, migrations (delegating to the existing schema_migrations ledger), MCP registration + auth token self-load, seed user + RBAC. Each step exposes check / apply / explain. The four entry points become thin callers selecting a step profile, so a fix lands once. Ship `doctor` as the flagship: run all checks, print exactly what is broken and the one command to fix it — replacing today's guess-and-patch debugging.

## What it unlocks
Ends the fix-one-path-break-another cycle (a dozen PRs/month of it); gives the Self-Host & Operate roadmap theme (ce7e2773) its core artifact — for an open-core project post-launch, install-success *is* the product's front door, and `doctor` converts every future setup bug report into a self-diagnosis; makes worktree and CI provisioning trustworthy for agents (several recorded agent failure modes are bootstrap drift).

## Rough size
5–8 days including migrating all four paths and deleting the superseded script logic. Touches scripts/, tools/ or packages/ (new package), docker compose entrypoints, .github/workflows, docs.

## Migration risk
The main risk is breaking the paths that currently work while porting them — mitigated by migrating one entry point at a time with the old script kept as fallback for one release each, and by `doctor` being additive from day one (pure reads). Rollback per path: repoint the entry script at its previous implementation.

## The strongest argument against
The patch storm coincided exactly with public-launch preparation — a one-time event. If setup churn drops to near zero next month on its own, this builds a framework to solve a problem that just finished existing; shell scripts that now work are cheaper to keep than a bespoke setup engine that itself needs tests, docs, and maintenance. A fair alternative is to wait one month: if the setup-fix rate stays materially above zero post-launch, build it; if not, only extract `doctor` as a read-only script and stop there.
Promoted 2026-11-21 to plan 5d225120-b187-439c-9c4f-7caf35eb03f9 (One bootstrap engine behind every setup path, plus a workspace doctor). This plan owns the engine. Standalone-install plan 4bec3d8e (desktop bundle) does not; it would consume a profile. Setup churn continued after 11-15 (#932, #883, #876), and there is no workspace doctor, only telemetry:doctor.

Write skill script: destroy.sh (worktree removal)
Net-new — a repo-wide grep confirms there is NO worktree-removal logic anywhere today (no `git worktree remove`, no prune, no server-side teardown). Removal is currently manual, which is why orphan worktrees pile up.

Add `skills/ot-worktree/scripts/destroy.sh` as the third composable action alongside `create.sh` and `heal.sh`. It must be usable standalone AND callable from the other two.

Invocation modes, mirroring `create.sh` so the three feel like one tool:
1. Name as `$1` — resolve to `<root>/<name>` via the same `resolve_worktree_root` ladder from `root.sh`. Never guess a path; if the resolved path is not a registered linked worktree of this repo, fail loudly.
2. Absolute path as `$1` — remove that worktree.
3. No args, run from INSIDE a linked worktree — self-removal. Must `cd` to the primary checkout before removing, since you cannot delete the directory you are standing in.

Behavior:
- Refuse to run against the primary checkout. This is the single most important guard in the script — a bug here deletes the user's actual repo. Assert `is_linked_worktree` for the target and that the resolved path is present in `git worktree list --porcelain` for this repo's common dir. Bail with a clear error otherwise.
- `git worktree remove <path>`; on failure due to a dirty tree, do NOT silently `--force`. Report what is dirty (`git -C <path> status --short`) and require an explicit `--force` flag from the caller. Uncommitted work in a worktree is the exact thing that must not be destroyed by accident.
- Delete the branch only when explicitly asked (`--delete-branch`), and then only if it is merged — `--delete-branch --force` for the unmerged case. Default: leave the branch alone.
- `git worktree prune` afterwards so stale admin dirs in `.git/worktrees/` do not linger.
- Run a repo teardown hook if one exists, BEFORE removal, using the same discovery shape as `provision.sh`: `$OT_WORKTREE_TEARDOWN`, then `.worktree/teardown.sh`. No `scripts/` fallback (there is no incumbent to preserve). Nothing found → no-op. Pass the same env (`OT_SOURCE_REPO`, `OT_WORKTREE_NAME`, `OT_WORKTREE_PATH`), stdin closed. A teardown that exits non-zero aborts the removal — this is where a repo stops a container or releases a port lease, and removing anyway would leak it.
- A `--dry-run` flag that prints exactly what would be removed and exits 0. Given how destructive this is, make it easy to check first.
- Stdout stays quiet (path or nothing); diagnostics on stderr, matching the other two scripts.

Factor the "is this really a removable linked worktree of this repo" check into `common.sh` so `create.sh`'s provision-in-place mode and `heal.sh` can share the same notion of a valid target.

Then wire it up: add a `worktree:remove` script to `package.json` pointing at `./skills/ot-worktree/scripts/destroy.sh`, and document all three actions (create / heal / destroy) in SKILL.md as the composable set. Note in `references/contract.md` that a repo may provide `.worktree/teardown.sh` as the mirror of `.worktree/provision.sh`.
destroy.sh added: name/path/self-removal modes, --dry-run, --force, --delete-branch. Guards verified — the primary checkout and an unregistered path are both refused with the registered-worktree list printed, via the new shared is_registered_worktree() in common.sh (registered + linked + not the primary). Teardown hook runs before removal and aborts on non-zero; removal runs from the primary checkout so self-removal works; git worktree prune afterwards; branch preserved unless --delete-branch (merged-only without --force). package.json gains worktree:remove.

Spike: pin the per-OS detection mechanism and the trust signal
**No production code.** The whole feature is worthless if the probe is confidently wrong, so establish what actually works before building around it.

1. **Verify the macOS trap empirically.** On a machine with VS Code installed, check whether `code` is on PATH. It ships opt-in via "Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH", so confirm the failure mode is real rather than taking the plan's word for it. Then find a reliable bundle check: `/Applications/Visual Studio Code.app`, `~/Applications/…`, and whether `mdfind kMDItemCFBundleIdentifier == 'com.microsoft.VSCode'` is worth the spawn cost. Record actual bundle ids for all three editors (VS Code, Cursor, Claude Code) — read them off the installed apps, do not guess.

2. **Decide the trust signal.** The plan proposes keying `unknown` off the container-bridge env (`OPENTHROTTLE_HOST` / `CONTAINER_WORKSPACES_DIR`, the same vars `toContainerPath` reads). Confirm those are actually set in the containerized deployment — read the docker-dev config rather than assuming. If they are not a reliable indicator, find one that is. **Getting this wrong is the worst outcome in the plan:** a container reporting `not_found` tells users their working editor is missing.

Handle the already-installed branch of the setup command
## Resolved with no code change, deliberately

The task's own goal — "the recording needs a way to get the fresh-install output without uninstalling the operator's own MCP config" — is already met by the script as it stands. `renderInstructions(root, status)` takes `status` as a **parameter** with `detectInstallStatus()` only as its default:

```ts
const renderInstructions = (root: string, status: InstallStatus = detectInstallStatus()): string
```

That signature exists precisely so the install state can be supplied rather than sniffed. The demo surface calls `renderInstructions('/workspace/openthrottle', { claude: false, cursor: false })` and gets the fresh-install rendering on a machine where OT MCP is very much installed. No on-disk state is read, nothing is written, and the operator's `~/.claude.json` and `~/.cursor/mcp.json` are never touched.

## No flag was added, and that is the finding

The task offered "a flag or an env override that forces the not-installed rendering, added to the script rather than faked in the flow". Both were rejected:

- The parameter already **is** the seam. A `--force-fresh` flag or an `OT_MCP_ASSUME_FRESH` env var would be a second, redundant way to reach the same code path, and every added path is a new way for the default behaviour to regress — which the task explicitly forbids.
- An env override is worse than a flag here: it would make the command's output depend on ambient state, so a stale export in the operator's shell could silently print install instructions to someone who does not need them.

Using the parameter is not "faking it in the flow" either — the flow does not hand-write the block, it calls the product's own renderer. The distinction the task was guarding against is a pasted copy of the output, and that is exactly what is *not* happening.

## Contract is already under test

`scripts/__tests__/setup_mcp-instructions.test.ts` covers the path the surface depends on: `renderInstructions(ROOT, NEITHER)` naming both clients and embedding the resolved launcher, the already-installed branch, the all-installed branch, and — usefully for gate 2 — "every placeholder value is a literal `${...}` token". So the surface is not depending on an untested private detail; it is depending on asserted behaviour.

The one guard that did NOT exist is a test that the *rendered surface text* stays leak-clean. That is a demo-tree concern rather than a script concern, so it is implemented with the surfaces in task 4 rather than bolted on here.
RESOLVED WITH NO CODE. renderInstructions(root, status) is already an exported pure function with tests covering the both-false path, so the recording forces the fresh-install rendering by passing status. No flag added — deliberately.

knip config: register the Docker-invoked MCP HTTP entrypoints so they stop reporting as dead
Follow-up from task `96f1c030`, which was SKIPPED this run because its "safe to delete" verdict was wrong.

## Problem

`packages/openthrottle-mcp/src/bin-http.ts`, `src/run-server-http.ts`, `src/http/mcp-http-auth.middleware.ts`, `esbuild.http.mjs`, and the package's `esbuild` devDependency are all load-bearing for the containerised streamable-HTTP MCP surface:

- `Dockerfile.NestJS:155` (`mcp-development` stage) — `CMD ["sh", "-c", "node_modules/.bin/tsx packages/openthrottle-mcp/src/bin-http.ts"]`
- `Dockerfile.NestJS:181` (`mcp-build` stage) — `RUN node packages/openthrottle-mcp/esbuild.http.mjs`
- `Dockerfile.NestJS:192` (`mcp` distroless stage, "the shippable image") — `CMD ["bin-http.mjs"]`
- `docker-compose.yml:497` `mcp` service (prod profile, `image: openthrottle/mcp:latest`) and `docker-compose.yml:531` `mcp-dev` service (`develop.watch` hot reload)

Because knip only follows the TypeScript import graph and these are shell-invoked container entrypoints, knip reports the whole cluster under `Unused files` and `esbuild` under unused devDependencies — every single weekly sweep. That recurring false positive already produced one task instructing deletion, whose ADDENDUM wrongly asserted the Docker grep was clean. Deleting would have broken the `mcp`/`mcp-dev` compose services and stripped the published image's entrypoint.

## Work

Teach knip about the entrypoints rather than re-triaging them by hand each week. In the knip config that covers `packages/openthrottle-mcp` (the `monorepo:knip` target's config):

1. Add `src/bin-http.ts` to the package's `entry` patterns, so `run-server-http.ts` and `http/mcp-http-auth.middleware.ts` become reachable through the normal import graph and drop off the report on their own.
2. Add `esbuild.http.mjs` to `entry` (it is a build script invoked by `node`, not imported), which should also clear the `esbuild` devDependency hit. If it does not, add `esbuild` to that project's `ignoreDependencies`.
3. Leave a short comment at each addition naming the Dockerfile stage that invokes it, so the next reader does not have to re-derive why a file with no importer is an entry.

While there: check whether the same blind spot affects the other Docker/CI-invoked entrypoints the plan description already lists as known false positives (`bootstrap.ts`, `ensure-migrations.ts`, `generate-mock-mail-fixture.mjs`, `sync-subtree.sh`). If they are cheap to declare the same way, do it in this pass — the point is to shrink the recurring manual-triage surface, not just to patch this one cluster.

## Acceptance criteria

- `pnpm nx run monorepo:knip` no longer reports `bin-http.ts`, `run-server-http.ts`, `http/mcp-http-auth.middleware.ts`, or `esbuild.http.mjs` as unused files, and no longer reports `esbuild` as an unused devDependency for `openthrottle-mcp`.
- No source file under `packages/openthrottle-mcp/src` is deleted or modified by this task — it is a config-only change.
- `docker compose --profile prod build mcp` still builds (or, if Docker is unavailable in the working environment, confirm by inspection that no Dockerfile/compose reference was touched).
- `pnpm nx run @openthrottle/openthrottle-mcp:build` and `:test` stay green.
The openthrottle-mcp HTTP cluster is a shipped Docker entrypoint with no in-repo importer, so knip reports it as unused every sweep — it nearly got deleted this run. Declare the entrypoints in knip config instead.

```
beats: 0:00 0:07 0:15 0:24 0:33 0:41 0:49   ·   source: 01-what-is-openthrottle.md

### payoff-first  (127 words)

]
```

2. Developer root: lazy-load GlobalMetrics/recharts (1650.8 KB shared)
## Finding
Every `openthrottle-developer` route pays a **2253 KB** base shell because `root.tsx` eagerly imports `GlobalMetrics`, which pulls `recharts` into a shared client chunk.

## Paths
- `applications/openthrottle-developer/app/root.tsx` (imports `GlobalMetrics`)
- `packages/react-router-ui-global/src/components/GlobalMetrics.tsx`
- `packages/react-router-ui-global/src/components/GlobalMetricsChart.tsx` (`import { LineChart, … } from 'recharts'`)
- Built: `applications/openthrottle-developer/build/client/assets/src-BD*.js` (**1650.8 KB raw / 470.5 KB gzip-9**; fingerprints recharts/cmdk/sonner/vaul). Referenced by `root-*.js`.

## Measured before
```bash
pnpm nx run openthrottle-developer:build
# base shell = entry+jsx+root+src-BD*+runtime+react+rollbar ≈ 2253 KB
# src-BD*.js alone: 1650.8 KB raw / 470.5 KB gzip
```
Home (`_index`) total ≈ **2266 KB**; usage/dashboard ≈ **2274 KB** — charts are paid even when the metrics panel is closed.

## Suspected cause
Eager `GlobalMetrics` → `GlobalMetricsChart` → `recharts` from the app shell. Commander (`cmdk`) and toaster/drawer libs ride the same shared chunk.

## Proposed fix
Lazy-load `GlobalMetrics` / `GlobalMetricsChart` (dynamic import when the metrics panel opens). Split recharts out of the root-shared chunk. Keep commander/toaster reviews secondary once recharts is gone.

## Expected after
- Root-shared vendor chunk containing recharts **absent** from the initial graph
- Base shell (same composition as above) **≤ 1200 KB raw** (target: remove ≥400 KB gzip from first load)

## Acceptance
Production build: `src-BD*.js` (or successor shared chunk) either drops below **800 KB raw** or no longer contains `recharts` / `LineChart`; `root-*.js` has no static import of the metrics chart module. Re-measure base shell < 1200 KB.

Decide how the cold open shows a rule firing
The script's first beat is "add the tag `needs-review` to the plan; a rule fires and a toast shows" over "I added one tag. Something just happened on its own." This is the hook, and `docs/marketing/youtube-format.md` treats the first three seconds as where retention is decided - so it cannot be quietly softened.

`queues/plan-rules/plan-rules.processor.ts` is a BullMQ worker: one job is one full evaluation pass over a plan, loading the plan owner's enabled rules, running the pure evaluator, dispatching matched actions through `ActionExecutorRegistry` and reconciling the ledger. Nothing in that path pushes anything to the browser. Adding a tag revalidates the plan; the rule's effect lands out of band.

Option A (recommended) - re-time the beat. Add the tag, hold, and let the injected task appear on the plan when the pass completes. "Something just happened on its own" is MORE true when it happens with no further click, and this teaches the real mental model instead of implying a synchronous UI reaction. Costs the flow a `waitFor` on the injected task rather than a fixed dwell, and costs the take some non-determinism.

Option B - open on the aftermath: start on a plan that already carries the tag and the injected task, then show why. Safest to record, weakest hook.

Option C - surface rule application as a live notification. Real product work well outside a screencast plan; if it is wanted, it should be its own plan and this one blocks on it.

Record the decision and the reasoning here before task 3 starts.
DECISION: option A, re-timed further. No client feedback path exists at all (no toast; PlanRuleApplications commented out; InjectTaskExecutor emits no notification, so the plan page does not live-update). The flow adds the tag, dwells while the worker runs, then RE-OPENS the plan and waits on the injected task title. Verified live 2026-08-26.

12. BUG: @vscode/ripgrep unresolvable from the built SSR bundle (IDE routes broken in production)
## Finding
Found while doing task 4 — **not a regression, pre-existing on `main`.** Importing the built `ide-engine.server-*.js` chunk from a production server build throws at module load:

```
Could not find @vscode/ripgrep-darwin-arm64.
Ensure optionalDependencies are installed for this platform (darwin-arm64).
```

The platform package **is** installed (`node_modules/.pnpm/@vscode+ripgrep-darwin-arm64@1.18.0` exists in both this worktree and the main checkout). The problem is resolution scope, not installation.

## Reproduction
```bash
pnpm nx run openthrottle-developer:build --skip-nx-cache
cd applications/openthrottle-developer/build/server
node -e "const p=require('node:fs').readdirSync('assets').find(f=>f.startsWith('ide-engine.server-'));import('./assets/'+p).then(()=>console.log('OK')).catch(e=>console.log('FAILED:',e.message.split('\n')[0]))"
```
Verified this fails **identically with and without** the task-4 `ssr.external: ['ts-morph']` change (stashed the vite config, rebuilt, same error), so it predates that work.

Also:
```bash
cd applications/openthrottle-developer && node -e "require('@vscode/ripgrep')"   # Cannot find module
cd <repo root>                       && node -e "require('@vscode/ripgrep')"   # Cannot find module
```

## Root cause
`@vscode/ripgrep` is a dependency of `@openthrottle/openthrottle-ide`, so under pnpm's strict layout it only resolves from inside that package's own `node_modules`. Vite **bundles** `openthrottle-ide` into the SSR chunk (it is source-first, `main: ./src/index.ts`), and the bundled ripgrep shim then does a runtime lookup for its native binary relative to the bundle's location — `applications/openthrottle-developer/build/server/assets/` — where neither `@vscode/ripgrep` nor its platform package is reachable.

Because this throws at **module load**, it takes down every tier of the IDE engine, including the ts-morph tiers that never touch ripgrep.

## Impact
All `/ide` routes (`ide._index`, `ide.files`, `ide.symbol`, `ide.symbols`) fail on a production build. Dev mode works, which is why this has gone unnoticed.

## Proposed fix
Same shape as the task-4 fix: add `@vscode/ripgrep` to `applications/openthrottle-developer/package.json` dependencies and mark it `ssr.external` in the app's `vite.config.ts`, so Node resolves both it and its platform-specific optional dependency from the app's own `node_modules` at runtime. Confirm the Docker image ships the matching `linux-x64`/`linux-arm64` optional dep.

## Acceptance
The reproduction command above prints `OK`, and `listFilesVM` / `searchVM` return real results against a checkout on a production build.
Plan: 🔁 Performance: 2026-08-21

Everything about that was designed for one repo — this one. Running in someone else's checkout raises questions the current core does not answer:

1. **Which server?** How does a hook running in an arbitrary repo discover the OT endpoint — env var, plugin-bundled config, spawn-time injection? What if the operator runs several OT servers?
2. **How is the repo identified and scoped?** `scope.ts` resolves scope today from monorepo assumptions. What is the identity of a foreign repo in the telemetry — remote URL, path, a registered `WorkspaceLocalRepository` row?

Answers the four questions: (1) endpoint — the `<repoRoot>/.env` legs of resolveGraphqlUrl/resolveAuthToken are DISABLED in foreign repos (reading a stranger's .env is both a privacy violation and a correctness bug); permitted sources are SKILL_USAGE_* overrides → process env (how leg B supplies it, since the driver owns the child env) → `~/.openthrottle/hooks.json` (how leg A supplies it); never the plugin dir, which must stay operator-agnostic and byte-stable. Teach scripts/parallelize-tasks.ts about per-suite sharding without breaking the round-trip
The real work. Today `scripts/parallelize-tasks.ts` answers exactly one question — "which projects are mine?" — and deals every affected project to exactly ONE chunk. `openthrottle-developer:test` now needs to run on ALL THREE boxes with different `--shard` arguments, which cuts across that contract.

## Constraints that must survive

- **`getShardSelectionErrors()` must keep holding.** Its whole point is that a project cannot silently fall off every box while CI reports green. If the developer app is special-cased out of the `--exclude` selector for `test`, the round-trip check must be taught about that exception explicitly rather than having the exception quietly widen `unexpected`.
- **`lint`/`typecheck` stay on the existing project-partition path.** They are 5.5% and 6.1% of the heavy box; they do not need this and must not be destabilised by it.
- The script's stdout remains the machine-read contract (single line, empty = empty shard); diagnostics stay on stderr.
- The header JSDoc's "Deliberately NOT parameterized by target" rationale is about the quoting hazard (no argv slot may contain a space). If this change introduces a second output, keep that property or rewrite the rationale honestly — do not leave the comment asserting something that stopped being true.
- The `!project` direct-naming warning (vs `!tag:name:`) still applies to anything new that builds a selector.

## Two shapes to choose between (task 2's decision may force one)

- **A — special-case out:** the app is removed from the `test` partition entirely and the workflow runs its sharded `test` unconditionally on every box. Simplest partitioner change; the round-trip check needs an explicit allowance.
- **B — shard-aware partition:** the partitioner grows a notion of per-project shard assignment and emits, alongside the exclude selector, this box's shard argument for the sharded project. Keeps one source of truth for "who runs what", at the cost of a second output channel.

Pick one, and write down why the other was rejected — the next person will ask.

## Also handle

- The developer app is only sharded when it is IN the affected set. On a PR that does not touch it, nothing should shard and no box should invent work.
- Interaction with `distributeEvenly()`: with the heaviest app pulled out of the `test` deal, the applications-first bias is rebalancing against a different weight distribution. Note it; do not re-tune it here.

## Tests

Extend `scripts/__tests__/parallelize-tasks.test.ts` (it already covers `getIsPackage`, `splitProjects`, `getChunkIndex`, `distributeEvenly`, `getExcludeSelector`, `getShardSelectionErrors`, `getShardSelector`). New cases must include: developer app affected vs not affected; every affected project still covered exactly once across the three chunks; and the round-trip check still failing loudly on a genuinely dropped project.

## Done when

`pnpm nx run monorepo:test` is green, the new behaviour is unit-tested, and the exported surface is still pure/testable with the Nx calls confined to `verifyShardSelection()` / `getAffectedProjects()`.

Handle the untrusted / all-unknown probe honestly
`detectEditorPresence` returns `trusted: false` with every editor `unknown` when the server is containerized (bridge mapping or `/.dockerenv` / `/run/.containerenv`), when the platform is not darwin, or when the probe threw. The `trusted` field is already selected by the `getEditorPresence` document but nothing in the UI reads it — the row simply vanishes, which is indistinguishable from "the query failed" and from "no editors were found".

Add, in `WorkspaceEditorPresenceHints`, a single low-key line rendered **only** when the probe returned `trusted === false` (or every entry is `Unknown`): a one-sentence note that OpenThrottle cannot inspect this machine from where the server is running, so no detection is being claimed. New copy key in `WORKSPACE_SETTINGS_COPY`.

This requires passing the full `editorPresence` object (not just `.editors`) into the hints component — widen the prop, keeping `null` meaning "query failed, render nothing at all". Note the distinction the component must now hold: `null` → render nothing; `trusted: false` → render the note, no chips; trusted with entries → render chips.

Consider surfacing `scannedAt` as a relative timestamp on the row — decide yes/no and record the reasoning in the task summary rather than leaving it silently dropped. Bias toward no if it adds noise; the probe runs per page load, so it is always fresh.

Tests: cover all three states in `WorkspaceEditorPresenceHints.test.tsx`.
Prop widened from `editors` to the full `presence` object, and the component now holds three outcomes apart instead of collapsing them into one silent row: `null` → nothing (no result to characterize); `trusted: false` OR every entry UNKNOWN → the new `presenceUntrustedNote` line, no chips (`data-testid="WorkspaceEditorPresenceUntrusted"`); trusted with a real claim → chips, with individual UNKNOWN entries still filtered out. Treating all-unknown the same as explicitly-untrusted is deliberate: the server had nothing it was entitled to claim either way. scannedAt: NO — the probe runs per page load behind a short soft TTL, so a relative timestamp would read "just now" on every render, which is noise that implies staleness the user never has to reason about. It's documented in the component JSDoc and pinned by a test asserting no timestamp leaks into the markup. 6 outcome tests + the existing suite migrated.

Column manifest: every exported column classified, schema drift fails the export
The fail-loud guard, relocated from seed time to export time. A committed manifest beside the exporter classifies every (table, column) in the export scope as keep (verbatim), scrub (through the identity/secret pass), or drop (nulled or omitted), and every table in the database as exported | denied | ignored — each entry with a one-line reason.

Before writing anything, the exporter reflects the live schema (information_schema.columns, pg_constraint) and compares:

- a **table not in the manifest** (new migration) fails: "table X is not classified — decide exported/denied/ignored";
- a **column not in the manifest** on an exported table fails naming table and column;
- a **manifest entry whose column no longer exists** (rename/drop) fails, reported as a rename/drop rather than a bare Postgres error;
- a **vector column whose dimension changed** since the snapshot was committed fails, so a model/dimension change cannot silently strand stale embeddings.

This manifest is deliberately the first draft of the deny list a future public read-only guest instance will need — write it as if it will be promoted.

Done when: each failure case above is reproduced in a test against a scratch database or mocked reflection, with a specific, actionable message.
A committed keep/scrub/drop manifest over the export scope; an unclassified column or table stops the export naming it.

Decide the MCP-flag posture: unconditional vs per-surface
This is a design decision, deliberately sequenced before any driver implementation — getting it wrong means reshaping the capability signature after five drivers have already adopted it.

`buildShellCommand` has three consumers:

- scheduled jobs — `applications/openthrottle-server/src/queues/scheduled-agent-jobs/scheduled-agent-runner.service.ts`
- chat — `packages/openthrottle-agentic-utils/src/utils/conversation-backend/agent-setup-executor.ts:220`
- Ralph — `tools/workflows/src/bin/run-iteration.ts:109` (and `:125`)

`--trust` / `--approve-mcps` auto-approve every configured MCP server. For an unattended scheduled run in a known repo that is exactly the intent. For an interactive chat session it may widen what the agent can reach without the user's knowledge.

Establish, then decide:

1. **Baseline** — does chat already get `openthrottle-mcp` today? Start a chat from the developer app against the cursor backend and ask it to enumerate MCP servers. If it already works, determine whether that is because the CLI attaches automatically in that mode, or because a one-time interactive trust prompt was answered on this machine — the latter means the current behavior is unreproducible on a fresh checkout, which argues for the flags.
2. **Same question for Ralph** via `tools/workflows/src/bin/run-iteration.ts`.
3. **Decide the shape.** Either:
   - *Unconditional* — driver capability alone gates the flags. Simplest; acceptable only if step 1 shows chat already has equivalent access.
   - *Per-surface* — the flags are threaded through the invocation config (an explicit field on `RunAgentPromptConfig` / `DriverInvocationConfig`), so scheduled runs and Ralph opt in while chat keeps the narrower posture. More plumbing, but honest.

Deliverable: the chosen shape, with the concrete type signature the driver tasks will implement, recorded in the plan output stream. The next task implements against that signature rather than inventing one.

Note the constraint from `no-deep-package-imports`: anything new is consumed via the package main entry and re-exported from `index.ts`.
Settle whether MCP flags are always-on or threaded per invocation surface BEFORE the capability signature is designed and five drivers adopt it.

Fresh worktrees cannot run any documented `pnpm exec workflow-*` command
In a worktree created with `pnpm run worktree:new <name>`, `node_modules/.bin/workflow-ralph` (and `workflow-lighthouse`, `workflow-link-merge`) do not exist. In the primary checkout they do.

**Re-verified 2026-08-30 — the root cause is structurally unchanged, though the file moved.** Provisioning was rewritten in TypeScript since this was filed (`scripts/setup_worktree.sh` is now a thin tsx shim over `scripts/setup_worktree.ts`), but the ordering defect survived the rewrite verbatim: `scripts/setup_worktree.ts` runs `step('pnpm', ['install'])` at **line 250** and `step('pnpm', ['build'])` at **line 253**. `tools/workflows/package.json` still declares its three bins as `./dist/src/bin/*.js`, so at link time the targets still do not exist and pnpm still skips creating the shims.

Re-running `pnpm install` afterwards does not repair it — pnpm reports "Already up to date" and exits, and `pnpm install --force` does the same (both verified on a fresh worktree; the package's `dist/src/bin/*.js` were present and executable, timestamped one minute *after* the install).

Effect: `pnpm exec workflow-ralph …` fails with `Command "workflow-ralph" not found` in any fresh worktree, so every documented `pnpm exec workflow-*` invocation is broken there until someone rebuilds and reinstalls. Worked around during the smoke runs by invoking `node tools/workflows/dist/src/bin/ralph.js` directly.

Fix at the root — either order the install after the build, or add an explicit relink step to the provisioning script. Do not paper over it by rewriting the docs to call `node dist/...`.

**One scoping note before starting:** `@tools/workflows` now carries a `deprecated` field in its `package.json` directing new code to `@openthrottle/nestjs-agentic-workflow`, and describes `workflow-ralph` as "a thin local CLI shim", with `workflow-link-merge` and `workflow-lighthouse` "staying here until relocated". Check whether these three bins are being relocated before investing in the fix — if they are moving to a package that builds differently, fix the install/build ordering anyway (it is a general provisioning defect that will bite the next `dist`-bin package) but do not spend effort on `@tools/workflows`-specific plumbing that is about to be deleted.

Acceptance: a worktree created fresh via `pnpm run worktree:new` has working `workflow-ralph`, `workflow-lighthouse`, and `workflow-link-merge` shims in `node_modules/.bin`; `pnpm exec workflow-ralph --help` succeeds there with no manual repair.
Still live: scripts/setup_worktree.ts installs (line 250) before building (line 253), so pnpm skips the @tools/workflows bin symlinks and a later install reports "Already up to date" without repairing them.

Reduce checkout cost: stop full-cloning a 47 MB repo on every job
Every job uses `fetch-depth: 0`, a full-history clone of a 47 MB repo, three-plus times per CI run. Real time and (on paid runners) real money, plus bandwidth on every run.

- `build` genuinely needs history for `nrwl/nx-set-shas` to locate the last successful `main` run.
- `changes` does not (covered by task 4).
- `nx-dependency-graph` and the gated `vercel-deploy` jobs should be audited the same way.

Options for the jobs that do need history:
1. `filter: blob:none` on `actions/checkout` — a partial clone fetches commit/tree objects but not historical blobs. Usually the best fit for `nx affected`, which needs the commit graph, not old file contents.
2. A bounded `fetch-depth` large enough to reach the base SHA, with a fallback deepen when it is not found. More fragile — prefer option 1.

Verify `nx affected` still computes an identical project set before and after on the same commit pair; a silently-wrong affected set would under-test rather than fail loudly, which is the dangerous outcome here.
